title: OSH Code: safety, health and working conditions
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Thirteen older laws merged into one Code on safe workplaces.
body:
The **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020**, usually called the OSH Code, is the Labour Code that decides how safe a workplace must be and what basic conditions every worker can expect: hours, leave, welfare facilities and a written appointment. It is the widest of the four Codes in terms of the laws it replaces. This post explains what it says, who it covers, what is new for contract and migrant workers, and what to watch as it is put into practice.

## Background: thirteen laws in one

The OSH Code consolidates 13 earlier laws. Among them are the Factories Act, the Mines Act, the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, the Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act and the Building and Other Construction Workers Act. Each of those Acts had its own inspectors, registers, licences and definitions. A single construction project could fall under several of them at once. The Code's aim is one set of rules, one registration and one licence wherever possible.

According to PRS Legislative Research, the Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 19 September 2020, passed there on 22 September and passed by the Rajya Sabha on 23 September 2020.

## Who is covered

The general provisions apply to establishments with **ten or more workers**, and to any establishment doing a notified hazardous activity regardless of size. Mines and docks are covered without a worker threshold. For factories, the Code sets the threshold at 20 workers where power is used and 40 where it is not, compared with 10 and 20 earlier. Mines are no longer excluded from the factory definition. Law-firm summaries point out that the thresholds in different parts of the Code are not uniform, which is something rules will need to make clear.

## Contract labour

Contract workers are among the most exposed to accidents, and also among the least protected by written terms. The Code applies the contract labour provisions to establishments or contractors employing **50 or more** contract workers, up from 20. Contractors need a licence, which can be tied to a particular project or work.

Contract labour is prohibited in **core activities**, with exceptions: where the establishment's normal functioning ordinarily uses contractors, where the work does not need a full-time workforce for most of the day, or where a sudden increase in work must be completed within a fixed time. The appropriate Government decides what counts as core, and the Bill lists activities such as sanitation and security as non-core. If a contractor fails to pay wages, the principal employer is responsible for paying them.

## Inter-State migrant workers

Millions of workers move between States for jobs in construction, textiles, brick kilns and other trades. The Code treats an inter-State migrant worker as one who earns up to Rs 18,000 a month, or a higher figure the Central Government notifies, and it now includes workers who travel on their own and find work in another State, not only those recruited by a contractor. Employers must provide:

- a **journey allowance**, which the Code makes an annual entitlement, so that the worker can travel home once a year;
- suitable working conditions and medical facilities.

A migrant worker can choose to draw Public Distribution System entitlements in the home State or the State of work. A portal keeps a record of such workers, and they may register themselves using Aadhaar. The 2019 draft's displacement allowance, equal to half the monthly wages, was removed from the final text.

## Hours, leave and basic duties

- The maximum working day is **eight hours**, with weekly holidays and annual leave with wages.
- Overtime is payable at twice the normal rate and needs the worker's consent, according to one law-firm summary.
- **Appointment letters** are to be given to every worker, setting out the terms of employment. This is a simple provision with large practical value: a worker with a letter can prove that she was employed, at what wage and from what date.
- No child below 14 may work, and in mines the minimum age is 18.
- Employers must provide a safe, risk-free workplace, train workers in safety procedures and, in certain industries, appoint medical officers. Mine owners and agents share joint responsibility for safety.
- Workers in hazardous processes are entitled to **annual health check-ups**.

## Women at work

The Code allows women to be employed in all establishments and in all types of work. For night work, between 7 pm and 6 am, the conditions are the woman's consent, the employer's responsibility for safety, security and dignity, and adequate transport. For hazardous work, the Government may require safeguards. Supporters see this as widening choice. Unions will want to see that consent is real and that transport and security arrangements are in place and checked.

## Enforcement

The Code places inspection in the hands of **Inspector-cum-Facilitators**, who can inspect, investigate accidents and, where workers are in danger, restrict or prohibit work. The appropriate Government may exempt establishments for a notified period, and State Governments can exempt new factories to encourage employment. Civil courts are barred from hearing matters under the Code. A person who is aggrieved must use the appellate authority or approach a High Court by writ petition. Penalties can be compounded at 50 per cent of the maximum fine for fine-only offences, and some compounded amounts and penalties go to a Social Security Fund for unorganised workers.

## Why safety is a labour issue

Deaths and injuries at work make headlines only when they are large, such as a mine collapse or a factory fire. Yet each accident is a family that has lost an earner. For BMS, safety is a matter of dignity and not only of compliance, and its sector unions regularly raise accidents in mines, construction and manufacturing. A union that insists on proper helmets, ventilation, training and compensation is doing the work the law expects.

## What BMS has asked

In its pre-Budget letter of 6 January 2025, reported by Organiser, BMS asked the Government to remove what it considers anti-worker provisions from the Industrial Relations Code and the OSH Code, and notify the rest. It also asked that contract workers be regularised, and that the Government set an example as an employer.

## What to watch

- **State rules.** The Code is a central law, but inspection is largely a State function. A law-firm note stresses that full operation needs matching State notifications.
- **The strength of inspection.** Trained inspectors, web-based and random inspection, and a worker's ability to complain without losing the job all matter.
- **Contract workers.** They carry the highest risk, and the line between core and non-core work will be argued about for years.
- **Exemptions.** How freely the Government grants exemptions will decide how much protection actually reaches new factories.

## A later update

The Ministry of Labour and Employment announced that the four Labour Codes would come into effect on 21 November 2025. Readers should check the notified Central and State Rules for the current position.
